newsitem.title: INDIA: Warring northeast Indian tribals go on killing spree.
newsitem.headline: Warring northeast Indian tribals go on killing spree.

text.p: More than 60 people have been killed in a sudden escalation of violence between two rival tribal groups in the north-east Indian state of Manipur during the past two weeks, police said on Tuesday.
Armed Kuki tribesmen massacred Naga families in a series of raids on villages in the Churachandpur district, they told Reuters from the state capital of Imphal.
Clashes between the two tribes have left more than 1,000 people dead since mid-1992.

The history of the strife is rooted in a mix of territorial battles, the Nagas' fight for independence from India, a lucrative drug trafficking racket, and a bloody spiral of revenge killings, security sources said.
"Most of the affected areas are deserted, like ghost towns and houses destroyed," one senior police officer said.
"With the security personnel patrolling the hills and tension still prevailing, no one wants to return to their homes."
Despite a heavy security force presence, the violence has gone unchecked. Armed groups can easily move unseen in the hilly, forested terrain.
Manipur, a remote state of one million people bordering Burma, is home to three major ethnic groups and numerous other sub groups.
An influx of Kukis, a migrant tribe from Chin state in Burma, has reduced the Nagas to a minority, particularly in Churachandpur district.
Nagas, fiercely independent former head hunters, have fought for a homeland since India won its own freedom from Britain 50 years ago.
They occupy more than 10,000 sq. km (6,250 sq. miles) of mountainous territory covering four north eastern Indian states and the Saging Division of Burma, between Hukuang and Brahmaputra valley.
Manipur is the gateway between India and Southeast Asia, and one of the main drug trafficking routes from the Golden Triangle areas of Burma.
Indian security sources say many of the armed groups in the area are involved in the trade.
They estimate that some $840 million worth of narcotics are carried every year on the highway through Manipur from the Burmese border to the neighbouring state of Nagaland.
More than half a dozen militant Kuki groups are fighting for control of the highway. The Nagas have fewer armed outfits.
Naga students and human rights organisations have accused the Indian government of using the Kukis in a proxy war against their people.
"It is the government which is providing arms to kill our people," Artax A. Shimray, a Naga leader said.
Others said revenge motivated the Kukis.

"There is no question now that government is taking revenge on Nagas through Kukis, it's the Kukis taking revenge for killing hundreds of their people and for houses destroyed during 1992 and 1993," a senior church leader, who requested not to be named, told Reuters in Guwahati.
Both tribes were converted to Christianity by colonists.

Local efforts to bring peace to the region have so far failed. Immediately after leaders of the two ethnic groups signed a peace agreement on Monday, Kuki militants massacred 25 Paities, a sub group of Nagas, in a village near Singtam area of the district.
More than 700 Paitie Nagas are now in relief camps set up
in the Churchandpur district.
